# posthog_feature_flags (Data Source)

List the feature flags in a project. Use this to resolve the numeric `id` of each flag that already exists, so a `for_each` `import {}` block can adopt them into `posthog_feature_flag` resources. Deleted flags are left out, as are the flags PostHog creates internally for surveys and product tours. Archived flags are included, because an archived flag still holds its key and creating a new flag with that key fails.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# List the flags in a project.
data "posthog_feature_flags" "all" {
  project_id = "12345"
}

output "active_flag_keys" {
  value = [for flag in data.posthog_feature_flags.all.flags : flag.key if flag.active]
}

# Promote flags from dev to staging to production, adopting flags that already
# exist instead of creating duplicates, without writing any flag IDs.
#
# Each environment has its own PostHog project and its own Terraform state, and
# the same configuration is applied to each in turn, for example from CI:
#
#   terraform -chdir=flags init -backend-config=dev.backend.hcl
#   terraform -chdir=flags apply -var environment=dev
#   # ...then the same with staging, then production
#
# A flag created by hand in a project's UI is adopted by the import block on
# that environment's next apply; anywhere it does not exist yet, it is created.
variable "environment" {
  type = string

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "production"], var.environment)
    error_message = "environment must be dev, staging or production."
  }
}

locals {
  # Every flag, declared once. A feature ships to dev first and is rolled out
  # further as it moves towards production.
  feature_flags = {
    "new-onboarding" = {
      name    = "New onboarding flow"
      rollout = { dev = 100, staging = 100, production = 25 }
    }
    "beta-dashboard" = {
      name    = "Beta dashboard"
      rollout = { dev = 100, staging = 50, production = 0 }
    }
  }
}

resource "posthog_project" "this" {
  name = var.environment
}

# Looked up by name, because a new environment's project ID is not known until
# apply. Until the project exists this finds no flags, so every flag is created.
data "posthog_feature_flags" "existing" {
  project_name = var.environment
}

resource "posthog_feature_flag" "this" {
  for_each           = local.feature_flags
  project_id         = posthog_project.this.id
  key                = each.key
  name               = each.value.name
  rollout_percentage = each.value.rollout[var.environment]

  # If the environment already had a project with this name before Terraform
  # managed it, import that project first: see project_name above. This turns
  # the replace that would otherwise delete its flags into a plan-time error.
  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }
}

# for_each in an import block needs Terraform 1.7 or later. Once a flag is in
# state its import does nothing, so the block can stay in place.
import {
  for_each = {
    for flag in data.posthog_feature_flags.existing.flags : flag.key => flag.id
    if contains(keys(local.feature_flags), flag.key)
  }
  to = posthog_feature_flag.this[each.key]
  id = "${data.posthog_feature_flags.existing.project_id}/${each.value}"
}
```

## Schema

### Optional

- `organization_id` (String) Organization to look `project_name` up in. Defaults to the provider-level organization_id. Requires `project_name`.
- `project_id` (String) Project ID (environment) to list flags in. Defaults to the provider-level project_id. Conflicts with `project_name`. When the project is looked up by `project_name` and none matches, this is null.
- `project_name` (String) Name of the project to list flags in, matched case-insensitively within `organization_id`. Use this when the project ID is not known until apply, for example a project created in the same configuration. When no project has this name, `flags` is empty rather than an error. More than one project with the name is an error. If a project with this name already exists, import it into your `posthog_project` resource rather than creating a second one: before the new project exists, this name matches the old one, and adopting its flags into resources pointed at the new project plans to replace them. Terraform deletes the old flags before PostHog refuses the second project, so they are lost even though the apply fails. Setting `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` on the flag resources turns this into an error at plan time.

### Read-Only

- `flags` (Attributes List) The project's flags, sorted by key. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--flags))

<a id="nestedatt--flags"></a>
### Nested Schema for `flags`

Read-Only:

- `active` (Boolean) Whether the flag is enabled.
- `archived` (Boolean) Whether the flag is archived.
- `id` (Number) Numeric ID of the flag. Use `<project_id>/<id>` as the `id` in an `import {}` block.
- `key` (String) Flag key.
- `name` (String) Flag name (its description in the PostHog UI).
